strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: personalizing predictions for new federated clients without labeled adaptation data or local gradient updates. Separating client-level expert selection from per-example routing is a sensible design.

Anchor-client supervision provides an interesting mechanism for stabilizing specialization when clients receive only a subset of experts. The objectives and pseudocode make the main algorithm understandable.

The reported results are promising: Table 1 reaches 95.7% on CIFAR10 and 78.6% on CIFAR100 with two downloaded experts, while pretrained expert initialization reaches 83.27% on CIFAR100 in Table 2. These results improve on the common expert itself.

The appendix adds substantive experiments, including Dirichlet partitions, overlapping anchor labels, matched expert counts, and changing client populations. The ablations on feature quality and anchor frequency expose useful failure conditions rather than reporting successes alone.
weaknesses: The baseline results need stronger validation before supporting the headline superiority claims. On CIFAR10, Table 1 reports FedAvg at 58.4% and FedMix at 42.9% despite a 93% common expert; SCAFFOLD collapses to chance. Appendix B.1 explicitly identifies learning-rate inconsistency with pretraining as one explanation for FedAvg deterioration. Documented validation-based tuning, checkpoint selection, and implementation checks are needed. Against the frozen 93% model, FedJETs' improvement is approximately 2.7 percentage points, substantially smaller than its advantage over the deteriorated baselines.

The anchor mechanism relies on consequential assumptions that are not operationally resolved. Appendix A constructs anchors using controlled label distributions, while the main experiments allocate half of each round's participants to only five or ten anchors. Constructing these clients is different from identifying suitable anchors among existing private clients. The overlapping-label experiment helps, but does not establish robustness to unrepresentative anchors or limited availability. These issues matter because performance degrades substantially without anchor sampling.

The contribution needs clearer differentiation from prior federated mixture-distribution methods, particularly FedEM, and stronger isolation of its proposed mechanism. Appendix H's visualization of label-frequency K-means does not establish that clustering or mixture approaches are unsuitable. Appendix F usefully controls expert counts, but comparisons with anchor-only specialists and routing alternatives under the same anchor schedule would help distinguish the benefits of routing, auxiliary supervision, and concentrated training.

The evidence for generality and efficiency is limited. Evaluation uses two related image datasets, synthetic label shifts, and 100 training clients; unseen label combinations do not establish robustness to broader domain shifts. Sending K rather than M experts offers a clear communication advantage over downloading the full bank, but the paper does not quantify total bytes, computation, memory, or latency, including the common feature extractor. Communication rounds alone do not establish the claimed overall efficiency or scalability.

Important reproducibility and statistical details are missing: the exact common-expert pretraining data and procedure, checkpoint availability, local sample counts and overlap, router dimensions, baseline search spaces, and repeated-run uncertainty. The manuscript supplies no code link. Several appendix tables report the best test accuracy during training without describing a separate validation-based selection protocol, making the reported advantages harder to assess reliably.

Some claims require clearer definitions and qualification. Section 4 claims near-perfect expert selection, but Table 4 reports 27.1% CIFAR100 error without adequately defining routing correctness or distinguishing it from classification error. The unconditional privacy wording also exceeds the evidence: keeping raw data local does not establish privacy of communicated expert selections and model updates. These are unresolved support and clarity issues, rather than evidence of demonstrated ethical misconduct.
